title: Model Distillation
shortDefinition: A technique for training a smaller, faster model to replicate a larger model's behavior.
definition: Model distillation (also called knowledge distillation) is a technique for training a smaller, faster 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger, more capable 'teacher' model — capturing much of the teacher's performance in a more efficient package that costs less and runs faster at inference time. Distillation is a key technique for deploying capable AI in cost-sensitive or latency-critical contexts where running the full-size original model isn't practical.

sections.title: How model distillation works
sections.description: The student model is trained to mimic the teacher model's output patterns, capturing more information than raw labels alone.

content.text: In distillation, the smaller student model is trained not just on the original labeled data, but specifically to mimic the larger teacher model's output patterns — including the nuanced probability distributions the teacher model produces, which contain more information than just the single 'correct' label. This additional signal helps the smaller model learn more effectively than it would training on raw labels alone, often achieving performance meaningfully closer to the teacher model than its smaller size would otherwise suggest is possible.

items: Student model — smaller, faster target model.
Teacher model — larger, more capable original model.
Output pattern mimicry — student learns from teacher's full output distribution.
Additional signal — probability distributions contain more information than raw labels.
Efficiency gain — smaller model captures much of the teacher's capability.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Distillation captures the teacher model's nuanced output patterns — not just correct answers, but the full probability distribution that contains richer learning signals.

sections.title: Why model distillation matters for production economics

content.text: A large, highly capable model often costs significantly more per inference call and runs slower than a smaller model — at production scale, this cost and latency difference compounds substantially. Distillation lets you capture much of a large model's capability in a smaller package, reducing inference cost and latency for high-volume production use cases, or enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices where the full-size original model simply wouldn't run efficiently or at all.

items: Inference cost reduction — smaller models cost less to run.
Latency improvement — faster inference for better user experience.
Edge deployment — enables models on resource-constrained devices.
Scale economics — savings compound with production volume.
Capability preservation — maintains much of the large model's performance.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of model distillation

content.text: Model distillation has limitations. There is almost always some accuracy loss compared to the larger teacher model, though distillation typically preserves more than training from scratch. Distillation requires access to the teacher model's outputs, which may not be available for some proprietary models. The process adds upfront cost and time, and distilled models may not be as general as the original for new or edge cases. Distillation also requires careful validation to ensure the smaller model remains reliable for your use case.

items: Accuracy loss — some capability gap is almost always present.
Teacher access — need access to teacher model outputs.
Upfront cost — distillation adds time and expense.
Generalization risk — distilled models may be less general.
Validation needed — careful accuracy testing is required.
Task suitability — not all models are good candidates for distillation.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about model distillation

items.question: How much smaller is a distilled model compared to the original?
items.answer: This varies significantly by use case and target deployment constraints; ClickMasters scopes the right size reduction for your specific cost, latency, or edge deployment requirements.

items.question: Is model distillation the same as fine-tuning?
items.answer: No — fine-tuning adapts a model's behavior for a specific task; distillation trains an entirely smaller model to replicate a larger model's behavior, often for cost or deployment efficiency reasons rather than task adaptation.

items.question: Does distillation always reduce accuracy compared to the original model?
items.answer: Generally some capability gap exists between the distilled student and original teacher model, though distillation often preserves more performance than training a similarly-sized model from scratch would achieve.

items.question: When does model distillation make the most sense?
items.answer: When inference volume is high enough that cost/latency savings justify the upfront distillation investment, or when deployment constraints (edge devices, mobile applications) require a smaller model than the original.

items.question: How long does a model distillation project take?
items.answer: 10–22 weeks depending on use case complexity and deployment target.

items.question: Can a distilled model be further fine-tuned for a specific task afterward?
items.answer: Yes, distillation and fine-tuning can be combined — distilling for size/cost efficiency, then fine-tuning the smaller model for your specific task requirements.

items.question: What is the difference between distillation and quantization?
items.answer: Distillation creates a new, smaller model architecture that mimics the original. Quantization reduces the precision of an existing model's parameters (e.g., 32-bit to 8-bit). Both reduce model size but work differently — distillation often yields smaller models, while quantization is a simpler post-processing step.

items.question: Can distillation be used with LLMs?
items.answer: Yes — distillation is increasingly used for LLMs to create smaller, faster variants that retain much of the larger model's capability. This enables cost-effective LLM deployment for high-volume applications.

items.question: What is the difference between online and offline distillation?
items.answer: Offline distillation uses a static set of teacher outputs for training. Online distillation uses the teacher model during training, generating outputs on the fly. Online distillation is more flexible but computationally more expensive.

items.question: How do you choose the student model architecture for distillation?
items.answer: Student architecture should be smaller and faster than the teacher while capable of capturing its behavior. ClickMasters selects appropriate architectures based on your size and speed requirements.
